original_question: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space have an infinite-dimensional quotient with a Schauder basis?
target_in_paper: Section 10, Problem 14 (the Banach-Pelczynski separable quotient question): "Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space X has an infinite-dimensional quotient with a Schauder basis?"
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact target almost verbatim. It has the right quantifier (every infinite-dimensional Banach space), the right object sought (a quotient), and the right structure on that quotient (a Schauder basis). It also matches the paper's intended problem in Section 10 rather than the neighboring variant about long Schauder bases.
missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, the ambient Banach space should be named explicitly as X.
In Banach-space language, the quotient should be written explicitly as a Banach quotient X/Y for a closed proper subspace Y of X.
The paper places this in the non-separable/general setting: no separability assumption is imposed on X.
The paper adds no extra hypotheses such as reflexivity, dual assumptions, unconditionality, or special scalar-field restrictions beyond standard Banach-space conventions.

Immediately after Theorem 13, the paper reformulates the same issue as the separable quotient problem: whether every infinite-dimensional Banach space has a non-trivial infinite-dimensional separable quotient.
refined_question: For every infinite-dimensional Banach space X, does there exist a closed proper subspace Y of X such that the quotient Banach space X/Y is infinite-dimensional and has a Schauder basis?
equivalent_formulation: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space have a non-trivial infinite-dimensional separable quotient?
justification: Section 10 explicitly says that the last four sections concern general Banach spaces without assuming separability, and then states Problem 14 in essentially the same words as your draft (Section 10, Problem 14, PDF p. 9). The nearby context says this is the "dual version" of the classical basic sequence problem (Section 10, opening paragraph, PDF p. 9). Theorem 13 then records the known positive result for every infinite-dimensional separable space, and immediately afterward the paper says, "So the problem of S. Banach and A. Pelczynski now becomes the following," namely Problem 15, the separable-quotient reformulation (Section 10, Theorem 13 and Problem 15, PDF p. 10). That makes your draft very accurate, with only the explicit quotient notation X/Y and the general/non-separable scope needing to be made fully explicit.
